title: The Teacher's Goodness and the Wings of the Soul
english: Regarding perfection, you say that his goodness is known when he instructs wise and perfect listeners; then his goodness is multiplied when he also descends to the simple, attempting to lead them into a greater state. Indeed, the teacher of Christianity is a debtor to the wise and the simple, to the Greeks and the barbarians. He is not only a debtor to the wise, but also to the simple.

To the wise he 'speaks wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor 2:6), but to the simple he does not speak wisdom, but rather proposes those lessons that remove them from thoughtlessness, so that they, no longer being simple, may later receive wisdom. Again, to the Greeks, he speaks as Greeks, those having a refined intellect capable of following; but as for the barbarians, regarding the soul, he says those things that remove the character of a barbarian nation, of such a wild disposition.

But the sons of men hope in the shelter of your wings (Ps 17:8). The sons of these men. If, according to the previous explanation, 'men' are said to be mortal rational animals and 'cattle' are those serving them, then the sons of these men have hope in the shelter of God's wings. These wings are intellectual, lifting the mind upward. Thus the saint says: 'Who will give me wings like a dove?' (Ps 55:6). We do not say that he prays to be given wings of a sensible animal; for this is impossible. And that which is impossible is neither love nor prayer.

'As an eagle upon its young ones has hovered' (Exod 19:4). Then they were winged, they were able to be taken up 'upon the transforming ones' of God. And what is it for us to be thus winged? Listen to what the prophet Isaiah says: 'Those who wait upon God shall renew strength, they shall fly up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary' (Isa 40:31). And another prays saying: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's' (Ps 103:5).

When the saint says of being winged, his wings are to be understood as virtue, understanding, and wisdom; for these things, as a catapult, lift man upward. 'They shall be covered from the heaviness of your house, they are covered under the wings of God.' Their shelter becomes the wings of God. Then they are covered so that they may become winged, so that they may be made healthy, as they might become under the wings of God. Their shelter becomes the wings of God.
unformed souls

title: The Soul as Multi-faceted Reality
english: It is the church of the living God. The richness of this house is perfect teaching, the wisdom spoken among the perfect, the 'solid food' of which the 'sensory' parts of the inner man partake, 'having been trained for the discernment of good and evil.' And these drink the wine harvested from 'the true vine.' Thus, these partake from the richness of this house of God. The richness of this house of God is perfect teaching, the unceasing knowledge of the truth.

And if he also calls the man the house of the Savior, since he says: 'destroy this temple' (John 2:19). 'This, he was speaking concerning the temple of the body,' not only that the body had a temple, but that this part of the temple could be destroyed by men. For he certainly took the destruction of the temple upon the body alone. But when he says: 'I lay down my soul, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18), he does not say: 'destroy my soul.' Thus they were saying something paradoxical: if he lays down his soul so that he may take it again, 'and no one takes it from him, but he himself has the authority to lay it down and take it' (John 10:18). Observe why: life was not taken from him by a common death. For certainly those crucified with him had their legs cut off so that they might die. Thus, without the Savior undergoing this, he was found dead. For 'bowing [his head], he surrendered the spirit' (Luke 23:46).

And if no one took the soul, but he himself laid it down from himself so that he might take it again, in this way, as it is said in one of the psalms: 'I became like a man helpless among the free dead' (Psalm 116:15), it has happened. And according to the immediate sense, we say that those being delivered from sins while 'being constricted by the chains of their own sins' are not free dead. Since, therefore, Jesus did not commit sin nor even knew it, he was free among the dead. Only this soul was seen to be free there. For certainly the gatekeepers of Hades flew it away.

According to a second sense, 'free among the dead' has happened thus: all those coming out of life and leaving the body, if they are diligent, are led by light-giving angels, while others are led by tormentors of some kind. For it has been said: 'the poor man died and was carried by the angels to the bosom of Abraham' (Luke 16:22). He did not become there by himself, but angels [carried] him.

Not led away. And to another animal-loving commentator it is said: 'O fool, in this night they demand your soul from you.' If a soul is demanded and is itself carried away to Hades by certain tormentors, only the soul of Jesus went out free; neither were angels requested to guide it, nor was it dragged away, not having the causes to be dragged. This indeed is to lay down and to take the soul, and 'no one took it' from me, he says, 'I have authority to lay it down, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18). The divine education by the Savior having become human is the sweetness of the house.

And the paradox: things said to be spiritual and intelligible are not paradoxical. Things that exist sensuously are not something else than sensible. But the being that is intelligible can also be sensibly perceived. It is therefore impossible to take the same high priest and lamb through sensation. But Jesus is both lamb and high priest. It is impossible to take the same door and house upon the sensible. But Jesus is both, and the door entering into the house, and that very house into which the door leads. And in a general sense, all intelligible things are such.

And concerning the soul of man, we say, that he cultivates himself, and the plant is the teaching, and that it is a ground receiving seeds and bearing fruit, and that it becomes a bride of the God Word and bears children of salvation. And it becomes also a sheep. And we take it according to various thoughts, names, and benefits. When the soul is called ground, the things capable are the seeds of certain teachings; but if it is called a bride, the women falling into it, and the cosmic things concerning it, are the practical and ethical virtues and the intellectual and perfect virtues. Again, when it is called a sheep, the teachings are called pasture, the educations are called grass. Therefore, all things are able at once to be other things and others.

And this must be understood: the so-called house is also a vine bearing wine; and again it is flesh nourishing; and it is a farmer tending plants so that they may bear fruit. And behold, that he himself is both farmer and vine and shepherd and sheep. According to various thoughts, being taken this way, they show that there is an intelligible essence concerning which these things are said. For instance, when a Greek demands: 'How can you show from your Scripture that, come, the soul is intelligible...'

title: The Vision of Light and Mercy to the Knowing
english: Is it so? For all things reported about it signify their own bodily properties, I was saying this: each of the bodies has that form according to which it is; but when it is spoken of in terms of participation, nothing is spoken of sensorially. God is called, Spirit is called, Light is called, as a man shaped and having limbs; for Spirit does not have limbs; God does not have a seat and a resurrection and feet and the rest; from which it is evident that the essences, about which these things are said, are certain things intelligible.

9 And you make them drink from the torrent of your delight. The flowing liquid is able toward quenching thirst and leading into a sober drunkenness. He names it a 'torrent of delight,' just as it is said, 'a river of delight issues forth from Eden and waters the paradise' (Gen 2:10). And the provision of teaching, the participation of instruction, is called 'torrents' of 'delight.' 'You make them drink upon it.' And it is well also to say, 'you make them drink upon it,' since after this torrent they come to be and are in that very spring. As infants they are being made to drink, and so that I may speak from apostolic wording: to those being led in, Paul writes, 'I gave you milk' (1 Cor 3:2). And those unable to drink for themselves are being made to drink; those being instructed are being made to drink. When they are made to drink from this river of delight, they consequently come to that life from which this river flows, 'for with you is the spring of life' (Ps 36:9). Since with you is the spring of life. He did not say, 'for with you the spring of life has become' or 'a spring of life shall exist,' but 'with you is the spring of life.' This spring of life is always. But when those being made to drink approach, a stream also flows and becomes from the spring, called the 'torrent of delight.'

10 For with you is the spring of life, in your light we shall see light. Behold the spring again here; he has spoken differently; and the light is spoken of as a spring. But these things are not possible regarding history or bodily imagination. If, therefore, the good things flow from it and it does not receive them from elsewhere like a pit or a head, it is a spring of life. And what am I saying? He himself was saying, 'I am the life' (John 14:6). It is the same to say 'life' and 'spring of life.' Life, indeed, because it vivifies and leads into immortality; but a spring, because it does not receive the vivifying thing from elsewhere, but has it itself within itself. 'In your light we shall see light.'

If this voice speaks to the Father, it says: since he who saw the Son, being true light, sees you as existing in light, in your own light we shall see you as existing in light; for 'he who saw the Son saw the Father' (John 1:18). And 'he is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15) indicating the one of whom he is the image, and 'he is the character of the divine hypostasis' (Heb 1:3) revealing the hypostasis of God. Therefore, 'in your light we shall see light'. And if this is also spoken to the Son, in your luminous instruction and teaching we shall see you existing as light.

Where he says: 'extend, O God, your mercy to those who know you' (Ps 103:8), he speaks of that knowledge concerning which it is said: 'this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God' (1 John 5:20). These ones, having this knowledge, are loved by God. And God 'makes mercy into thousands for those loving' him. We take 'into thousands' in this way: this number has a kinship with the unit. Therefore, those approaching the one God following and becoming one spirit with him, following, become thousands and myriads. But this is said in this sense: 'the chariot of God is myriad-fold, thousands of the straight'; for we do not take thousand in this way, as ten times a hundred, but because of the intimacy with the unit. And mercy becomes for them.

If, then, the mercy of God is extended into a thousand, as it is said: 'for his mercy is unto the age', he rightly says here: 'extend your mercy to those who know you'. Otherwise, he shows mercy to those coming in a manner of repentance, those asking for the forgiveness of sins. He shows mercy to those knowing him so that they may be established and ascend to that which is above all things unto the end. And your righteousness to the upright in heart. And upright in heart and pure in heart are the same. It is therefore good for the pure in heart to see God; for 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matt 5:8).
